definitions.text: Aaron was the son of Amram and Jochebed, of the tribe of Levi, and brother of Moses and Miriam (1 Chr 6:3). Because he spoke well, God appointed him to act as Moses' spokesman before Pharaoh (Exod 4:14; Exod 7:1), and the two led Israel out of Egypt together (1 Sam 12:6; Ps 77:20; Mic 6:4). He married Elisheba and had four sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. Aaron and his sons were consecrated as priests, with the office passing to his descendants (Lev 8:13; Exod 29:29; Heb 5:4). He made the golden calf while Moses was on the mountain (Exod 32:21; Acts 7:40). He died aged 123 on Mount Hor (Num 20:25; Num 33:39).
definitions.notes: Birth and death years (about 1574 and 1452 BC) are inferred from context and were omitted; only the age of 123 given in Num 33:39 is stated. Elisheba's parentage is not in the supplied verses, so only her name is given.

definitions.text: Abana was a river of Damascus, named by Naaman the Syrian army commander alongside the Pharpar when he objected to Elisha's instruction to wash in the Jordan: "Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?" (2 Kgs 5:12). It is mentioned only in that verse, and the text gives no further description beyond its link with Damascus, though Naaman's words imply he regarded it as a clean, abundant stream. It is probably the modern Barada River, which flows through Damascus in present-day Syria.
definitions.notes: Only one verse mentions Abana, and it supplies nothing beyond the name and its association with Damascus; the modern identification with the Barada is given as an inference. Some texts read "Amanah" in the margin, which is not reflected here.

definitions.text: Abiel was a Benjamite, son of Zeror, remembered as an ancestor of King Saul. In 1 Sam 9:1 Kish, Saul's father, is called the son of Abiel; 1 Sam 14:51 makes Ner, the father of Abner, a son of Abiel, while 1 Chr 8:33 and 9:39 say Ner fathered Kish. Reading these together, Abiel was probably Saul's great-grandfather, with "son" in 1 Sam 9:1 used loosely of a descendant. He is also identified with Jehiel, the founder of Gibeon, whose wife was Maachah (1 Chr 9:35), and so father of a large family including Abdon, Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zacher and Mikloth. The name Abiel belongs to more than one person in the Bible.
definitions.notes: The genealogies differ over whether Kish was Abiel's son or grandson; the definition treats Ner as the intervening generation by inference. The equation of Abiel with Jehiel of Gibeon, and the resulting list of children, rests on linking 1 Chr 9:35 with the Saul genealogy rather than on an explicit statement.

definitions.text: Ashur was a son of Hezron of the tribe of Judah, born to Hezron's wife Abiah after Hezron's death at Calebephratah (1 Chr 2:24). He is called "the father of Tekoa," which probably means he founded or settled the town of Tekoa rather than simply fathering a man of that name. He had two wives, Helah and Naarah (1 Chr 4:5), and through them a number of sons, including Ahuzam, Hepher, Temeni, Haahashtari, Zereth, Jezoar, Ethnan and Coz. His brothers were Jerahmeel, Ram and Caleb, and Segub was his half-brother through another of Hezron's wives.
definitions.notes: Only two verses mention him, and both are genealogical. The names of his sons come from the verses immediately following 1 Chr 4:5, which were not supplied as citable. The sense of "father of Tekoa" as town founder is an inference.

definitions.text: Atad was a threshing floor "beyond Jordan" where Joseph, his brothers and their Egyptian companions halted while carrying Jacob's body from Egypt for burial. There they held a great and bitter lamentation, and Joseph mourned his father for seven days (Gen 50:10). The Canaanites living in the area saw the mourning and said, "This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians," so the site was renamed Abel-mizraim (Gen 50:11). The exact location is unknown; the phrase "beyond Jordan" suggests a spot east of the river, though the funeral party was travelling toward Hebron, so a site west of the Jordan is also possible. Both verses are the only mentions of the name.
definitions.notes: Only two verses mention Atad, and no coordinates are known. The meaning of "beyond Jordan" here is genuinely ambiguous, so the geographic inference is deliberately hedged.

definitions.text: Baal-zephon was a place in Egypt used as a landmark for Israel's camp just before the sea crossing during the wilderness journey, dated by inference from context to about 1491 BC. God told Israel to turn back and camp by Pihahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon (Exod 14:2), and it was there that Pharaoh's chariots and horsemen overtook them (Exod 14:9). Num 33:7 repeats that Pihahiroth lay before Baal-zephon. The name suggests it was a site associated with the worship of a god called Baal, though the text does not say so. Its exact location is unknown; probably somewhere along the western side of the Gulf of Suez, in modern Egypt.
definitions.notes: All three verses mention Baal-zephon only as a geographical marker; nothing is said of the town itself. The identification with a site on the Gulf of Suez and the meaning of the name are inferences, flagged as such.

definitions.text: The birth of Simeon was the arrival of Leah's second son by Jacob, probably around 1757 BC by inference from context. According to Gen 29:33, Leah conceived again and bore a son, saying that the LORD had heard she was hated and had given her this son also; she named him Simeon. The passage links the name to the idea of being heard. The account reflects Leah's position as the less-loved of Jacob's two wives, and the naming follows the pattern of her other sons, whose names she explained by her circumstances.
definitions.notes: Only one verse supports the entry; the date is an inference from surrounding chronology, not stated in the text.

definitions.text: Cherith was a brook or seasonal stream valley where the prophet Elijah hid at God's command. He was told to go eastward and conceal himself "by the brook Cherith, that is before Jordan," and he did so (1 Kgs 17:3, 5). The phrase "before Jordan" suggests a ravine opening toward the Jordan River, and the instruction to travel east suggests a wadi on the river's eastern side, though this is an inference from the wording. Its exact site is unknown; it was probably one of the steep, seasonal torrent beds draining into the Jordan valley, dry for much of the year.
definitions.notes: Only two verses mention Cherith, and neither fixes its position beyond "eastward" and "before Jordan"; the proposed location east of the Jordan is inference, and sites on both sides of the river have been suggested.

definitions.text: The Creation of all things is the opening account in Gen 1:1–2:3, in which God makes the heavens and the earth over six days and rests on the seventh. The earth begins formless and dark, with the Spirit of God moving over the waters. God then speaks into being light; a firmament dividing the waters; dry land, seas and plants; sun, moon and stars; sea creatures and birds; land animals; and finally humankind, male and female, made in God's image and given dominion over living things and seed-bearing plants for food. God calls the finished work very good, then blesses and sets apart the seventh day. A traditional reckoning places it about 4004 BC, an estimate drawn from biblical chronology rather than stated in the text.
definitions.notes: The listed participants include Jesus Christ, but the supplied verses mention only God and the Spirit of God, so the definition does not name him.

definitions.text: Delilah was the woman in the valley of Sorek whom Samson loved (Judg 16:4). She repeatedly pressed him to reveal the source of his great strength and how he might be bound, accusing him of mocking her when his answers proved false (Judg 16:6, 10, 13). She tested each answer, once binding him with new ropes while men lay in wait in an inner room, but he snapped them like thread (Judg 16:12). When he finally told her everything, she summoned the Philistine rulers, who came to her bringing money (Judg 16:18) — implying, by inference from the passage, that she was paid for her part. The verses do not state her nationality or family.
definitions.notes: The supplied verses stop before the cutting of Samson's hair, so that outcome is not cited; her Philistine origin and the amount paid are not stated in the verses given.

definitions.text: The Deliverance by Ehud was Israel's escape from Moabite rule, achieved when Ehud son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite, killed Eglon king of Moab (Judg 3:15). Sent with tribute, Ehud carried a short two-edged dagger strapped to his right thigh, dismissed his companions, and returned claiming a secret message for the king. Alone with Eglon in his upstairs summer room, he drove the dagger into the very fat king, locked the doors, and slipped away while the servants waited (Judg 3:19-26). From the hill country of Ephraim he rallied Israel, seized the Jordan fords, and cut off the Moabites, killing about ten thousand men (Judg 3:27-29). Moab was subdued and the land had rest eighty years (Judg 3:30). This followed the subjugation under Eglon, about 1360 BC by inference from context.
definitions.notes:
The supplied duration of 62 years differs from the eighty years of rest stated in Judg 3:30; the verse figure is given in the definition. The dates are estimates inferred from context.

definitions.text: Fair Havens was a harbor on the coast of Crete, reached with difficulty by the ship carrying Paul toward Rome; the city of Lasea lay nearby (Acts 27:8). The name itself suggests a sheltered anchorage, and from the context of the voyage it appears to have been a stopping place rather than a major port. It is probably the site known today as Kaloi Limenes on the southern coast of Crete. The stop belongs to Paul's journey to Rome, about AD 56 by inference from context.
definitions.notes: Only one verse names Fair Havens; details of the delay there and the decision to sail on come from surrounding verses not supplied as citable, so they are not asserted here. The modern identification is given as inference.

definitions.text: Haggith was one of David's wives and the mother of Adonijah, listed as David's fourth son (2 Sam 3:4; 1 Chr 3:2). Her son was born during David's reign at Hebron, by inference from the list in 2 Sam 3. Haggith herself never appears as an actor in any scene; she is named only to identify Adonijah, who later declared himself king, gathered chariots, horsemen and runners, and was repeatedly called "the son of Haggith" (1 Kgs 1:5, 11; 1 Kgs 2:13). Nothing is recorded of her family, background or later life.
definitions.notes: All five verses name Haggith only as Adonijah's mother; nothing else about her is stated. The Hebron setting for Adonijah's birth is inferred from the surrounding list in 2 Sam 3.

definitions.text: Hezron was a place on the southern boundary of the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah. It is named only once, in Josh 15:3, where the border line runs up from the ascent of Akrabbim past Zin, climbs south of Kadesh-barnea, passes along to Hezron, goes up to Adar and turns toward Karkaa. Nothing else is said about it, and no event is recorded there. From its position in the list it was probably a settlement or natural landmark in the dry country south of Judah, near Kadesh-barnea, though its exact site is not known.
definitions.notes: Only one verse mentions the place, and it supplies nothing beyond a point in a boundary list. The supplied coordinates fall in Galilee, far north of the southern border context of Josh 15:3, so no modern identification is offered.

definitions.text: Jahath was a man of the tribe of Judah, son of Reaiah and grandson of Shobal. He was the father of Ahumai and Lahad, whose descendants made up the families of the Zorathites (1 Chr 4:2). Nothing else is recorded about him. Several different men in the Bible share the name Jahath, so this one is identified only by his place in this Judahite line.
definitions.notes: Only one verse mentions this Jahath; no dates, events or other details are available.

definitions.text: Jesus in Capernaum refers to Jesus leaving Nazareth and settling in Capernaum, a Galilean town on the lakeshore in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matt 4:13). Matthew links the move to words of Isaiah about the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, "by the way of the sea," where people sitting in darkness saw a great light (Matt 4:14–16). From that point Jesus began to preach, "Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" (Matt 4:17), and he taught in Capernaum on the sabbath days (Luke 4:31). The move followed his rejection at Nazareth. Dated to about AD 27 by inference from context; Capernaum is usually identified with a site on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee.
definitions.notes: The stated one-day duration does not fit Luke 4:31, which speaks of teaching on "sabbath days" and implies a longer stay; the definition treats the event as a relocation and the start of preaching rather than a single day.

definitions.text: Joseph (son of Judah) appears only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, where he is named as a son of Juda (Judah) and the father of Semei, whose line continues through Mattathias and Maath (Luke 3:26). Nothing else is said about him. Since the list traces ancestry toward David and Judah, he belonged by inference to the tribe of Judah. Several men named Joseph occur in this same genealogy, so he should not be confused with the others.
definitions.notes: Only one verse mentions him, giving nothing beyond his father, son and place in the list; tribal affiliation is an inference from the genealogy's wider context.

definitions.text: Lahmam was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah, named once in the Bible in a list of settlements in Judah's lowland district alongside Cabbon and Kithlish (Josh 15:40). Nothing further is said about it, and no event is linked to it. Its position within that list suggests it lay in the low hill country between the coastal plain and the Judean highlands, inland and southwest of Jerusalem; it is probably to be identified with a ruin site in that area, though the identification is an inference rather than something the text states.
definitions.notes: Only one verse mentions the place, and it gives no description beyond the name's position in a town list. The geographical placement and any modern identification are inferences from the surrounding names in the list.

definitions.text: The lifetime of Arphaxad spans the 438 years given for him in the family line from Shem to Abraham. He was 35 years old when his son Salah was born, and he lived 403 years after that, fathering other sons and daughters (Gen 11:12–13). Adding the two figures gives a total of 438 years. His birth is placed at about 2346 BC, an estimate inferred from the chain of ages in the surrounding chapter rather than a date stated in the text. No events of his life beyond these births are recorded.
definitions.notes: The total of 438 years is a sum of the two figures in Gen 11:12	a13; the text does not state it. The 2346 BC date is an estimate derived from the genealogical ages.

definitions.text: Michael was a Levite named in a genealogy of temple singers in 1 Chr 6:40. He was the son of Baaseiah and the father of Shimea, and his line is traced through the ancestry of Asaph. Nothing else is said about him; his place in the list is his only appearance. Several different men in the Bible share the name Michael, and this one is distinguished only by his father and son.
definitions.notes: Only one verse mentions him, and it gives nothing beyond his position in a genealogy. The connection to the singers' line and to Asaph is drawn from the surrounding list rather than from the verse itself.

definitions.text: The Mission to Iconium was a stage of Paul and Barnabas's first missionary journey, taking place in the city of Iconium, probably around AD 46 and lasting some months, by inference from context. The two went together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke so effectively that many Jews and Greeks believed (Acts 14:1). Jews who did not believe turned the Gentiles against them, but Paul and Barnabas stayed a long time, speaking boldly, with signs and wonders done by their hands (Acts 14:2-3). The city divided, some siding with the Jews and some with the apostles (Acts 14:4). When Gentiles, Jews and their rulers joined in an attempt to mistreat and stone them, the visit ended (Acts 14:5).
definitions.notes: The date (AD 46) and the five-month duration are estimates drawn from the sequence of the journey, not stated in the text; Acts says only "long time".

definitions.text: Mount Shapher (also spelled Shepher) was one of the stopping places where the Israelites camped during their journey through the wilderness. They came to it from Kehelathah and left it for Haradah (Num 33:23–24). Nothing else is said about the mountain, and its exact site is unknown; by inference from the order of the camps it probably lay somewhere in the desert country south of Canaan, perhaps in the region of the Arabah south of the Dead Sea.
definitions.notes: Only two verses mention the place, and both merely list it among the wilderness camps; the suggested location is an inference from the itinerary and approximate coordinates, not from the text.

definitions.text: Peter's Confession "Upon this Rock" was an exchange between Jesus and his disciples near Caesarea Philippi, about AD 29 by inference from context. Jesus asked who people said he was, and the disciples reported opinions that he was John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets (Matt 16:13–14; Mark 8:27–28; Luke 9:18–19). When he asked what they themselves thought, Simon Peter answered that he was the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matt 16:16; Mark 8:29; Luke 9:20). Jesus called him blessed, saying the answer came from his Father, named him Peter, said he would build his church on "this rock," and promised him the keys of the kingdom (Matt 16:17–19). He then told them to tell no one (Matt 16:20).
definitions.notes: Luke places the scene while Jesus was praying alone with his disciples and does not name Caesarea Philippi; the location comes from Matthew and Mark. Luke and Mark give a shorter form of Peter's answer and omit the "rock" and "keys" sayings.

definitions.text: Reaiah was the ancestor of a family of temple servants listed among those who returned from exile in Babylon. His descendants, "the children of Reaiah," appear in the registers of Ezra 2:47 and Neh 7:50, grouped with families such as Giddel, Gahar, Rezin and Nekoda. Nothing else is said of him; by inference from the context he lived before the exile and is known only through his descendants. The name belongs to more than one man in the Bible, so he should not be confused with others bearing it.
definitions.notes: Only two verses, both parallel name lists; the classification of his descendants as temple servants (Nethinim) is drawn from the surrounding list context rather than from the cited verses themselves.

definitions.text: Rehoboth was a city described as "Rehoboth by the river," the home of Shaul (also spelled Saul), one of the kings who ruled in Edom before Israel had a king. He became king after Samlah died (Gen 36:37; 1 Chr 1:48). The name Rehoboth is shared by more than one place in the Bible, and this one is identified only by its position beside a river, which is not named. Since the Edomite kings are listed together, the town probably lay in or near Edom, south-east of the Dead Sea, perhaps beside one of the seasonal watercourses there; others place it on the Euphrates. Nothing else is recorded about it.
definitions.notes: Only two parallel verses mention the place, and neither names the river. The supplied coordinates point to the Edom region, while an older identification places it on the Euphrates; both readings are noted as uncertain.

definitions.text: The Reign of Hezekiah covers the rule of Hezekiah son of Ahaz over Judah from Jerusalem, beginning in the third year of Hoshea of Israel (2 Kgs 18:1) — about 726 BC and lasting some 29 years, by inference from context. He did what was right in the LORD's sight, held to the LORD's commandments, and struck the Philistines as far as Gaza (2 Kgs 18:3, 18:6, 18:8). In his fourteenth year Sennacherib of Assyria took Judah's fortified cities and demanded tribute; his officer Rabshakeh taunted Jerusalem, but after Hezekiah prayed and consulted Isaiah, Sennacherib withdrew to Nineveh (2 Kgs 18:13–19:36). Hezekiah recovered from illness, received envoys from Babylon, and was succeeded by his son Manasseh (2 Kgs 20:7, 20:14, 20:21).
definitions.notes: The 726 BC start date and 29-year length are inferred from context, not stated in the cited verses; the sampled text covers 2 Kgs 18–20 only, so parallel accounts elsewhere are not reflected.

definitions.text: The reign of Jehoshaphat covers the twenty-five years in which Asa's son ruled Judah from Jerusalem, beginning in the fourth year of Ahab of Israel when Jehoshaphat was thirty-five, about 914 BC by inference from context (1 Kgs 22:41-42). His mother was Azubah, daughter of Shilhi. He followed his father's ways and did what was right in the LORD's eyes, though the high places stayed in use and the people kept offering there (1 Kgs 22:43). He removed those his father had left in the land (1 Kgs 22:46) and made peace with the king of Israel (1 Kgs 22:44). Edom then had a deputy rather than a king (1 Kgs 22:47). His trading ships for Ophir's gold wrecked at Ezion-geber, and he refused Ahaziah's offer of joint crews (1 Kgs 22:48-49). He was buried in the city of David, and his son Jehoram succeeded him (1 Kgs 22:50).
definitions.notes:
The summary rests only on the closing notice in 1 Kgs 22; fuller narratives of the reign elsewhere were not supplied. The date of about 914 BC is an estimate inferred from context.

definitions.text: Simeon was a man living in Jerusalem, described as just and devout and waiting for the consolation of Israel, with the Holy Spirit upon him (Luke 2:25). When Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the temple, Simeon blessed them and told Mary that the child was appointed for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and would be a sign spoken against (Luke 2:34). Nothing further is recorded of his family or later life. The name Simeon belongs to several different people in the Bible, so care is needed in distinguishing them.
definitions.notes: Only two verses supplied; the wider temple scene (his age, his song, his departure) is not included in the citable list, so the definition stays within what these verses state.

definitions.text: Tabor is a mountain in northern Israel, standing in the lower Galilee region near the border of Issachar and Zebulun; it is probably the isolated dome now called Jebel et-Tur, west of the Sea of Galilee. Josh 19:22 places it on the boundary of Issachar's territory, whose limits ran to the Jordan. Gideon questioned the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna about men they had killed at Tabor (Judg 8:18). Its prominence made it a byword: it is paired with Hermon in Ps 89:12 and likened to Carmel in Jer 46:18, both passages using the two peaks as markers of the land. Hos 5:1 accuses Israel's leaders of spreading a net on Tabor, by inference from the passage a figure for entrapment.
definitions.notes: Judg 8:18 does not say who killed the men at Tabor or when; the location of that event is given only by the name. The tribal attribution of Josh 19:22 to Issachar is drawn from the surrounding boundary list, not from the cited verse itself.

definitions.text: Zaccheus Converted and Parable of the Pounds took place as Jesus passed through Jericho, probably in a single day about AD 30 by inference from context, shortly after he healed blind Bartimaeus. Zacchaeus, a wealthy chief tax collector who was short, ran ahead and climbed a sycomore tree to see Jesus. Jesus called him down and stayed at his house, which caused the crowd to murmur. Zacchaeus promised half his goods to the poor and fourfold restitution for anything wrongly taken, and Jesus declared salvation had come to the house (Luke 19:8–10). Because Jerusalem was near and people expected the kingdom of God at once, Jesus told the parable of a nobleman who gave ten servants ten pounds. Then he went up toward Jerusalem.
